title: I. The Engagement
paragraphs: Once again Madame Hohlakov was the one who met Alyosha first. She was in a flutter, because something important had happened. Katerina Ivanovna’s hysterics had ended in a faint, and after that “a terrible, awful weakness had come over her. She lay there with her eyes rolled back, raving. Now she had a fever. They’d sent for Herzenstube and for the aunts. The aunts had already arrived, but there was no sign of Herzenstube yet. They were all sitting in her room, waiting. She was unconscious at the moment, and what if it turned into brain fever!”

Madame Hohlakov looked truly frightened. “This is serious, serious,” she kept repeating, every few words, as if nothing that had ever happened to her before had been serious. Alyosha listened unhappily and started to tell her what he had been through, but she cut him off after the first few words. She had no time to listen. She begged him to go and sit with Lise and wait there for her.

“Lise,” she whispered, almost into his ear, “Lise has given me a real surprise just now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch. She touched me, too, so my heart forgives her everything. Imagine, the moment you were gone she began to be honestly sorry that she’d laughed at you today and yesterday. She wasn’t laughing at you, mind, only joking. But she was seriously sorry, close to tears, and I was amazed. She has never been really sorry for laughing at me; she only turns it into a joke. And you know she laughs at me every minute of the day. But this time she meant it. She values your opinion very much, Alexey Fyodorovitch, so please don’t be offended or hurt by her, if you can help it. I’m never hard on her, because she’s such a clever little thing. Would you believe it? She said just now that you were a friend from her childhood, ‘the greatest friend of her childhood’—think of it—‘greatest friend’—and what am I, then? She has very strong feelings and memories, and what’s more, she has these phrases, these most unexpected words, that burst out suddenly when you least expect them. Lately she was talking about a pine tree, for instance. There used to be a pine tree in our garden when she was tiny. Very likely it’s still standing there, so there’s no need to use the past tense. Pine trees aren’t like people, Alexey Fyodorovitch; they don’t change quickly. ‘Mamma,’ she said, ‘I remember this pine tree as in a dream,’ only she put it in some way so original that I can’t repeat it. Anyway, I’ve forgotten it. Well, good-by! I’m so worried I feel I’ll lose my mind. Ah! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’ve lost my mind twice in my life. Go to Lise and cheer her up, the way you always can, so charmingly. Lise,” she cried, going to her door, “I’ve brought you Alexey Fyodorovitch, the one you insulted so. He isn’t angry in the least, I assure you; on the contrary, he’s astonished that you could think so.”
“_Merci, maman._ Come in, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”

Alyosha went in. Lise looked a little embarrassed and instantly turned crimson. She was clearly ashamed of something. And as people always do when that happens, she launched at once into talk about other matters, as though they absorbed her entirely at that moment.

“Mamma has just told me everything about the two hundred roubles, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and how you took them to that poor officer ... and she told me the whole dreadful story of how he’d been insulted ... and you know, mamma gets things muddled ... she’s always jumping from one thing to another ... but I cried when I heard it. So, did you give him the money, and how is that poor man?”

“The fact is, I didn’t give it to him, and it’s a long story,” Alyosha answered, as if he, too, could think of nothing but how sorry he was to have failed. But Lise saw perfectly well that he was looking away, too, and that he, too, was trying to turn the talk to something else.

Alyosha sat down at the table and began his story. At the very first words, though, his embarrassment left him, and he had Lise’s full attention as well. He spoke with deep feeling, still under the force of what he had just seen, and he managed to tell it well and with all the details. Back in Moscow he had loved to come to Lise and tell her whatever had just happened to him, or what he’d been reading, or something he remembered from his childhood. Sometimes the two of them had dreamed up stories together, whole romances, usually cheerful and amusing ones. Now both of them felt themselves suddenly carried back to those days in Moscow, two years ago. Lise was deeply touched by his story. Alyosha described Ilusha warmly. When he got to the part where the unlucky man trampled on the money, Lise couldn’t help clasping her hands and crying out:
“So you didn’t give him the money! You let him run off! Oh dear, you should have gone after him!”
“No, Lise, it’s better that I didn’t go after him,” said Alyosha. He got up from his chair and walked across the room, deep in thought.
“How is that? How can it be better? Now they’ve got nothing to eat, and there’s no hope for them?”

“There is hope, because the two hundred roubles will still get to them. He’ll take the money tomorrow. He’s sure to take it tomorrow,” said Alyosha, pacing up and down, thinking it over. “You see, Lise,” he went on, stopping suddenly in front of her, “I made one blunder, but even that has turned out for the best.”
“What blunder? And why for the best?”

“I’ll tell you. He’s a weak, timid sort of man; he’s suffered so much, and he’s very kindhearted. I keep asking myself why he took offense so suddenly. Because I assure you, right up to the last minute he had no idea he was going to trample on those notes. And now I think there was a great deal to offend him ... and in his position it couldn’t have gone any other way.... For one thing, he was sore that he had been so glad of the money in front of me, and hadn’t hidden it. If he’d been pleased, but not so very pleased; if he hadn’t shown it; if he’d started making a show of scruples and difficulties, the way other people do when they take money, then he might have managed to bear taking it. But he was too honestly delighted, and that was humiliating. Ah, Lise, he’s a good, truthful man, and that’s the worst of the whole business. All the time he was talking his voice was so weak, so broken. He talked so fast, so fast, and he kept laughing such a laugh, or maybe he was crying—yes, I’m sure he was crying, he was so delighted—and he talked about his daughters, and about the post he could get in another town.... And when he’d poured out his heart, he felt ashamed of letting me see right into his soul like that. So all at once he began to hate me. He’s one of those dreadfully touchy poor people. What shamed him most, you see, was that he’d given in too soon and taken me for a friend. At first he almost flew at me and tried to scare me off, but the moment he saw the money he began hugging me; he kept putting his hands on me. That’s probably how he came to feel it was all so degrading. And then I made that blunder, a very serious one. I suddenly said that if he didn’t have enough money to move to another town, we’d give it to him, and in fact I’d give him as much as he wanted from my own pocket. That hit him all at once. Why, he thought, was I shoving myself forward to help him? You know, Lise, it’s terribly hard on a man who’s been wronged when other people look at him as if they were his benefactors.... I’ve heard that; Father Zossima told me. I don’t know how to put it, but I’ve often seen it myself. And I feel it myself, too. And the worst of it was that although he didn’t know, up to the very last minute, that he would trample on the notes, he had a sort of presentiment of it, I’m sure of that. That’s exactly what made him so ecstatic, having that presentiment.... And dreadful as it is, it’s all for the best. In fact, I believe nothing better could have happened.”
“Why, why couldn’t anything better have happened?” cried Lise, staring at Alyosha in great surprise.

“Because if he’d taken the money, an hour after getting home he’d be weeping with mortification. That’s exactly what would have happened. And most likely he’d have come to me first thing tomorrow and maybe thrown the notes at me and trampled on them, as he did just now. But now he’s gone home terribly proud and triumphant, even though he knows he’s ‘ruined himself.’ So now nothing could be easier than getting him to accept the two hundred roubles by tomorrow, because he’s already proved his honor, tossed the money away and stamped on it.... He couldn’t know, when he did it, that I’d bring it to him again tomorrow, and yet he’s in terrible need of that money. Proud as he is of himself now, even today he’ll be thinking what a help he has lost. At night he’ll think about it more than ever and dream about it, and by tomorrow morning he may be ready to run to me and beg my forgiveness. And that’s just when I’ll turn up. ‘Look, you’re a proud man,’ I’ll say. ‘You’ve shown it; but now take the money and forgive us!’ And then he’ll take it!”
Alyosha was swept away with joy as he said those last words, “And then he’ll take it!” Lise clapped her hands.
“Ah, that’s true! Now I understand it perfectly. Ah, Alyosha, how do you know all this? So young, and he knows what’s in people’s hearts.... I’d never have worked it out.”

“The main thing now is to convince him that he’s on an equal footing with us, even though he takes money from us,” Alyosha went on in his excitement, “and not only an equal one, but even a higher one.”
“‘On a higher footing’ is charming, Alexey Fyodorovitch; but go on, go on!”
“You mean there’s no such expression as ‘on a higher footing’; but that doesn’t matter, because—”

“Oh, no, of course it doesn’t matter. Forgive me, dear Alyosha.... You know, until now I hardly respected you—that is, I did respect you, but only on an equal footing; now I’ll begin to respect you on a higher footing. Don’t be angry with me for joking, dear,” she put in at once, with strong feeling. “I’m silly and small, but you, you! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch. Isn’t there contempt in all this analysis of ours—I mean yours ... no, let’s call it ours—aren’t we looking down on him, on that poor man, by picking his soul apart like this, from above, as it were, eh? By deciding so surely that he will take the money?”

“No, Lise, it isn’t contempt,” Alyosha answered, as though he’d prepared for the question. “I was thinking about that on my way here. How can it be contempt, when we’re all like him, when we’re all exactly the same as he is? Because we are the same, you know, no better. And if we were better, we’d have done just as he did in his place.... I can’t speak for you, Lise, but I think my own soul is mean in many ways, and his isn’t mean; on the contrary, it’s full of fine feeling.... No, Lise, I don’t despise him. Do you know, Lise, my elder once told me to look after most people the way one looks after children, and some of them the way one looks after the sick in hospitals.”
“Ah, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, let’s look after people the way we would the sick!”
“Let’s, Lise; I’m ready. Though I’m not altogether ready in myself. Sometimes I’m very impatient, and other times I just don’t see things. It’s different with you.”
“Ah, I don’t believe that! Alexey Fyodorovitch, how happy I am!”
“I’m so glad to hear you say it, Lise.”

“Alexey Fyodorovitch, you’re wonderfully good, but sometimes you’re sort of stiff.... And yet you’re really not stiff at all. Go to the door, open it quietly, and see if mamma is listening,” said Lise, in a nervous, hurried whisper.
Alyosha went, opened the door, and reported that nobody was listening.

“Come here, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Lise went on, turning redder and redder. “Give me your hand—that’s right. I have a great confession to make. Yesterday I didn’t write to you as a joke, but seriously,” and she covered her eyes with her hand. It was plain that she was deeply ashamed of confessing it.
All of a sudden she seized his hand and, on impulse, kissed it three times.
“Oh, Lise, how wonderful!” cried Alyosha happily. “You know, I was absolutely certain you meant it.”
“Certain? Well, really!” She pushed his hand away but kept hold of it, blushing hotly and giving a happy little laugh. “I kiss his hand, and he says, ‘How wonderful!’”
But the reproach wasn’t fair. Alyosha was thoroughly flustered himself.
“I’d like to please you always, Lise, but I don’t know how to,” he mumbled, blushing as well.

“Alyosha, dear, you’re cold and rude. Do you see that? He’s picked me for his wife and he’s completely settled about it. He was sure I meant it. What a thing to say! That’s impertinence, that’s what it is.”
“Why, was it wrong to be sure?” Alyosha asked, suddenly laughing.
“Oh, Alyosha, no, it was wonderfully right,” cried Lise, gazing at him with tenderness and joy.
Alyosha stood still, her hand in his. Then he suddenly bent down and kissed her on the lips.
“Oh, what are you doing?” cried Lise. Alyosha was horribly embarrassed.
“Oh, forgive me if I shouldn’t have.... Maybe I’m terribly stupid.... You said I was cold, so I kissed you.... But I see it was stupid.”
Lise laughed and hid her face in her hands. “And in this dress!” she blurted out in the middle of her laughing. Then she stopped abruptly and became serious, almost stern.

“Alyosha, we’ll have to put off kissing. We’re not ready for it yet, and we’ll be waiting a long time,” she finished suddenly. “Tell me instead: you’re so clever, so intellectual, so observant. Why do you pick a little idiot, an invalid like me? Oh, Alyosha, I’m awfully happy, because I don’t deserve you one bit.”

“You do, Lise. I’m leaving the monastery for good in a few days. Once I go out into the world, I have to marry. I know that. _He_ told me to marry, too. Who could I marry better than you? And who would have me but you? I’ve thought it over. For one thing, you’ve known me since we were children, and you have many good qualities that I don’t. You’re lighter-hearted than I am, and above all you’re more innocent. I’ve already been brought up against so many things.... Ah, you don’t know it, but I, too, am a Karamazov. What does it matter if you laugh and make jokes, even at my expense? Go on laughing. I’m so glad when you do. You laugh like a little child, but you think like a martyr.”
“Like a martyr? What do you mean?”

“Yes, Lise. Your question a moment ago, whether we weren’t showing contempt for that poor man by taking his soul apart—that was the question of someone who suffers.... You see, I can’t put it well, but anyone who thinks about such questions is able to suffer. Sitting in your invalid chair, you must have thought over many things already.”

“Alyosha, give me your hand. Why are you pulling it away?” murmured Lise in a failing voice, faint with happiness. “Listen, Alyosha. What will you wear when you leave the monastery? What kind of suit? Don’t laugh, don’t be angry. It’s very, very important to me.”
“I haven’t thought about the suit, Lise, but I’ll wear whatever you like.”
“I’d like you to have a dark blue velvet coat, a white piqué waistcoat and a soft gray felt hat.... Tell me, when I said I hadn’t meant what I wrote, did you believe I didn’t care for you?”
“No, I didn’t believe it.”
“Oh, you impossible person, there’s no cure for you.”
“You see, I knew you—seemed to care for me, but I pretended to believe you didn’t, to make things—easier for you.”

“That’s worse! Worse, and better than anything! Alyosha, I’m awfully fond of you. Just before you came this morning, I tried my luck. I decided I’d ask you for my letter. If you took it out calmly and handed it over (just what you’d be expected to do), that would mean you didn’t love me at all, that you felt nothing and were only a stupid boy, good for nothing, and that I was ruined. But you’d left the letter at home, and that cheered me up. You left it behind on purpose, so you wouldn’t have to give it back, because you knew I’d ask for it? That’s how it was, isn’t it?”
“Oh, Lise, it wasn’t like that at all. I have the letter with me now, and I had it this morning too, in this pocket. Here it is.”
Alyosha pulled the letter out, laughing, and held it up for her to see from where he stood.
“But I’m not giving it to you. Look at it from there.”
“Why, so you told a lie? You, a monk, told a lie!”

“I lied, if you like,” Alyosha laughed too. “I lied so I wouldn’t have to give you back the letter. It’s very precious to me,” he added suddenly, with deep feeling, and he flushed again. “It always will be, and I won’t give it up to anyone!”
Lise looked at him with delight. “Alyosha,” she murmured again, “look at the door. Isn’t mamma listening?”
“All right, Lise, I’ll look. But wouldn’t it be better not to? Why suspect your mother of something so low?”

“What’s low about it? A mother spying on her daughter, that’s her right, it’s not low!” cried Lise, flaring up. “You can be certain, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that when I’m a mother, if I have a daughter like me, I’ll spy on her for sure!”
“Really, Lise? That’s not right.”

“Oh, my goodness! What has being low got to do with it? If she were listening in on some ordinary social conversation, it would be low. But when her own daughter is shut in with a young man.... Listen, Alyosha, I’ll have you know I’ll spy on you the minute we’re married. And I’ll tell you something more: I’ll open all your letters and read them. So you may as well be prepared.”
“Yes, of course, if that’s how it is—” muttered Alyosha, “only it’s not right.”

“Ah, how disdainful! Alyosha, dear, let’s not quarrel on the very first day. I’d better tell you the whole truth. Of course it’s very wrong to spy on people. Of course I’m wrong and you’re right. But I’ll spy on you all the same.”
“Go ahead, then. You won’t find out anything,” laughed Alyosha.
“And, Alyosha, will you give way to me? We have to settle that as well.”
“I’d be glad to, Lise, and I certainly will—only not in the most important things. Even if you disagree with me there, I’ll do my duty in the most important things.”

“That’s as it should be. But I’ll tell you, I’m ready to give way to you not only in the most important matters but in everything. And I’m ready to swear it right now—in everything, for the rest of my life!” cried Lise fervently. “And I’ll do it gladly, gladly! More than that, I swear I’ll never spy on you, not once, and never read a single one of your letters. For you’re right and I’m not. And though I’ll be terribly tempted to spy, I know I won’t, since you think it’s dishonorable. You’re my conscience now.... Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, why have you been so sad lately, both yesterday and today? I know you have a lot of worries and troubles. But I can see you have some special grief on top of that, a secret one, perhaps?”
“Yes, Lise, I have a secret one too,” answered Alyosha mournfully. “I can see you love me, since you guessed it.”
“What grief? What is it about? Can you tell me?” asked Lise, timidly pleading.
“I’ll tell you later, Lise—afterwards,” said Alyosha in confusion. “Right now you might not understand it—and maybe I couldn’t explain it.”
“I know your brothers and your father are worrying you too.”
“Yes, my brothers too,” murmured Alyosha, lost in thought.
“I don’t like your brother Ivan, Alyosha,” said Lise suddenly.
He took note of this with some surprise, but didn’t answer.

“My brothers are destroying themselves,” he went on, “and my father too. And they’re destroying others along with them. It’s ‘the primitive force of the Karamazovs,’ as Father Païssy put it the other day: a crude, unbridled, earthly force. Does the spirit of God move over that force? Even that I don’t know. I only know that I, too, am a Karamazov.... Me a monk, a monk! Am I a monk, Lise? You said a moment ago that I was.”
“Yes, I did.”
“And perhaps I don’t even believe in God.”

“You don’t believe? What’s the matter?” said Lise, quietly and gently. But Alyosha didn’t answer. These last words of his held something too mysterious and too much his own, perhaps unclear even to himself, and yet it tormented him.

“And now, on top of everything, my friend, the best man in the world, is going, is leaving the earth! If you knew, Lise, how closely my soul is bound to him! And then I’ll be left alone.... I’ll come to you, Lise.... From now on we’ll be together.”
“Yes, together, together! From now on we’ll always be together, all our lives! Listen, kiss me, I give you leave.”
Alyosha kissed her.

“Now go. Christ be with you!” and she made the sign of the cross over him. “Hurry back to _him_ while he’s still alive. I see I’ve been cruel to keep you so long. I’ll pray today for him and for you. Alyosha, we’ll be happy! Will we be happy? Will we?”
“I believe we will, Lise.”

Alyosha decided it was better not to go in to Madame Hohlakov, and he was leaving the house without saying good-by to her. But the moment he opened the door, there stood Madame Hohlakov right in front of him. From her very first word he guessed she had been waiting there deliberately to catch him.
“Alexey Fyodorovitch, this is dreadful. It’s all childish nonsense, and ridiculous. I trust you won’t imagine—It’s folly, nothing but folly!” she said, falling on him at once.
“Just don’t tell her that,” said Alyosha, “or she’ll get upset, and that’s bad for her right now.”
“Sensible advice from a sensible young man. Am I to take it that you only agreed with her out of pity for her being an invalid, because you didn’t want to upset her by contradicting her?”
“Oh, no, not at all. I was quite serious about what I said,” Alyosha declared firmly.
“To be serious about it is impossible, unthinkable. First of all, I shall never receive you here again, and I shall take her away, you may be certain of that.”
“But why?” asked Alyosha. “It’s all so far in the future. We may have to wait another year and a half.”

“Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that’s true, of course. You’ll have time to quarrel and part a thousand times in a year and a half. But I’m so unhappy! It’s such nonsense, yet it’s a terrible blow to me. I feel like Famusov in the last scene of _Sorrow from Wit_. You’re Tchatsky and she’s Sofya, and, just think, I ran down to meet you on the stairs, and in the play the fatal scene takes place on the staircase. I heard everything; I nearly collapsed. So that’s the explanation of her dreadful night and her hysterics lately! It means love for the daughter but death for the mother. I may as well lie in my grave right now. And something more serious still: what is this letter she’s written? Show it to me at once, at once!”
“No, there’s no need. Tell me, how is Katerina Ivanovna now? I have to know.”

“She’s still lying in delirium; she hasn’t come to. Her aunts are here, but all they do is sigh and put on airs. Herzenstube came, and he was so alarmed that I didn’t know what to do for him. I almost sent for a doctor to see to him. My carriage took him home. And on top of everything, you and this letter! It’s true that nothing can happen for a year and a half. In the name of all that’s holy, in the name of your dying elder, show me that letter, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I’m her mother. Hold it in your hand, if you like, and I’ll read it that way.”
“No, I won’t show it to you. Even if she allowed it, I wouldn’t. I’ll come tomorrow, and if you like, we can talk about many things. But now, good-by!”
And Alyosha ran down the stairs and out into the street.
